terms.definition: A grid of cells where each cell has a state, and every cell updates at the same time using the same rule based on its neighbors.
The eight cells touching a cell: up, down, left, right, and the four diagonals. Life counts live cells in this ring.
One tick of the simulation. Every cell looks at the old grid, and the whole new grid appears at once.
A short code for a Life-like rule. B lists the neighbor counts that give birth, S lists the counts that let a live cell survive. Conway's Life is B3/S23.
A pattern that never changes. Every live cell survives and no dead cell is born. Examples: block, beehive, loaf.
A pattern that returns to its starting shape after a fixed number of generations, called its period. Examples: blinker (period 2), pulsar (period 3).
How many generations a pattern takes to repeat itself exactly.
A pattern that returns to its own shape but shifted to a new spot, so it travels across the grid.
The smallest Life spaceship: five cells that move one square diagonally every four generations.
A pattern that stays in place and shoots out a new glider on a fixed schedule. Bill Gosper found the first one in 1970. It proved a Life pattern can grow forever.
A tiny starting pattern that churns for a very long time before settling down. The five-cell R-pentomino takes 1,103 generations.
Big-scale behavior that no single part was told to do. Gliders are not in Life's rules, but they appear from them.
Able to compute anything any computer can compute, given enough space and time. Life is Turing complete: gliders act as signals and collisions act as logic gates.
